beats.caption: Every link and certificate on the server rests on public-key crypto
beats.text: The TLS links, VPNs, code signatures and certificates on an AI server all depend on RSA and elliptic-curve keys. Their keys live in hardware security modules (HSMs). Most of that math is what a large quantum computer would break; the data encrypted today is what it would read later.

beats.caption: The new standards rest on lattice problems no quantum shortcut is known for
beats.text: NIST finalized ML-KEM (FIPS 203) for key exchange and ML-DSA (FIPS 204) for signatures in 2024. Both rest on lattice problems: find a short vector hidden in a grid of points. No known quantum algorithm solves them efficiently, so they are the replacement.

beats.caption: Shor's algorithm breaks RSA and elliptic curves outright
beats.text: Shor's algorithm finds the prime factors of an RSA modulus, and the discrete logs behind elliptic-curve keys, in polynomial time on a large enough quantum computer. The math that protects today's keys is the math that breaks, so the threat is to the keys themselves, not to their length.

beats.caption: Hybrid sessions hold both keys, so one weak link is not enough
beats.text: During migration a session runs a classical key exchange and a post-quantum one, then combines the secrets. The session stays secure as long as either holds. That is how browsers and cloud services are rolling out PQC first.

beats.caption: Certificates, chips and HSMs all need a multi-year upgrade
beats.text: The cost is in the replacement, not the math: certificates, firmware, HSMs and cloud services all change, and keys already recorded must be migrated. Vendors: IBM (IBM), Palo Alto Networks (PANW), Cloudflare (NET), Thales (HO.PA).
